title: Macquarie backs rival taking on big banks
full_text:
Macquarie has backed a non-bank challenger bucking the property downturn to take market share from the big four, as investors look to increase their exposure to low-risk credit.
The investment bank's commodities and global markets arm has joined Citi to stump up funding for non-bank lender Bridgit, which totals $1.7 billion and is carving out a niche in the softening lending market.
The profitable fintech allows property owners to unlock up to $10 million in home equity. Since it started five years ago, it has helped 10,000 borrowers bridge mortgages and transact more than $8 billion in property as it increasingly beats the big banks.
"Their processes are not set up to support shorter-term lending, and so for them, it's not an easy decision to be able to service and allocate enough resources to compete with us, and that's where we've been winning a lot of market share against traditional lenders," founder Aaron Bassin said.
The company has invested more than $15 million into an artificial intelligence-powered engine that could quickly assess a borrower's risk and approve loans in as little as two minutes, with about 80 per cent of business coming through its network of 20,000 brokers.
While Bassin identified its rivals as "predominantly" the big four, Bridgit also directly competed against Macquarie's banking and financial services division, which is growing its mortgage book faster than any other bank and also offers bridging loan products.
"We're pleased to increase this funding facility to Bridgit as it continues to meet growing demand for Australian home owners," Macquarie division director Alhad Bhalerao said.
It also gave Citi some skin in the game after it offloaded its consumer lending business in 2022 as part of a $1.2 billion sale to National Australia Bank. Bassin said the banks' investment was recognition of Bridgit's superior product and prospects.
Consecutive interest rate rises and the ongoing slide in national house prices have failed to disrupt its growth, with loan applications up 28 per cent over the past quarter as the fintech builds out a product suite it says can grow through the cycle.
"This time last year we were in a seller's market, and we had a lot of people looking to take advantage of a 'buy now, sell later' product to help them secure the new property before they sold because the market was moving so quickly," Bassin said.
"Now, in a buyer's market, people are taking advantage by upsizing to properties they previously couldn't afford."
Charging 8.5 per cent interest, at the top of a market where rates range between 6 per cent and 9 per cent, the fintech said it was finding demand amid renovations, separations and buyers waiting for the market to improve.
Lending more than doubled last year, while it signed a new partnership with ASX-listed aggregator Australian Financial Group in August to expand its funnel.
Bassin said the quality of the fintech's book, which has not had a single loss and runs on loan-value ratios of less than 60 per cent, was highly attractive to investors hunting in the Australian asset-backed securities market.
"Investors like Macquarie and Citi want high-growth businesses like Bridgit, where they are able to get exposure to a low-risk, low-LVR lending portfolio that's diversified across Australia," Bassin said.
